npcs.name: Vince

lines.text: Evening. Is this place open?
Open? Sweetheart, this place has never once been closed. Not for a storm, not for a blackout, not for the thing in eighty-one.
You go on in. Tall fella like you, they will comp you a room.
You are not surprised by me at all.
Pal, I work the door in this town. I stopped being surprised a long, long time ago.

topics.label: The suit does not bother you?
replies: Pal. We get four of you a week. Rabbit, bear, the fella who does the wolf and will not break character for a fire alarm.
Yours is better. I will give you that for nothing — yours breathes.
Right there at the collar. There is no gap. Every suit in this town has a gap at the collar and I have been looking at collars for twenty-two years.
So either you paid a great deal of money, or you did not. Either way it is none of my business and my feet hurt.

topics.label: Who actually owns this place?
replies: Officially? A company. The company is a name on a letterhead and the letterhead is a box number in a town that got flooded.
Unofficially, Halloran keeps the paper. Pit boss, inside, sees everything, admits to nothing.
Go and ask him about the deed. Go on. He has been sat on that thing for forty years waiting for somebody to walk in and ask him about the deed, and it is starting to affect him.

topics.label: Has anything strange ever happened on this door?
replies: Once every eight years the whole street goes dark and I stand here in it, because that is the job and the job does not stop for dark.
And every time — every single time — when it comes back up there is somebody standing at the kerb who was not there before, looking at the sign like they have lost something.
I say good evening. What would you do?

topics.label: Thanks, Vince.
replies: Go on in. And listen — if anybody asks, you came in through the front like everybody else.

npcs.bio: Doorman at big WIN casino. Twenty-two years on the same six feet of pavement.

npcs.name: Marla

lines.text: Ray. The licence is signed. That man has been holding our ring for an hour.
I know what he has been holding.
Then what are we waiting for?
The picture. I said we would see it again first, and I meant it when I said it, and I mean it standing here.
Ray. It is a picture.
It is THE picture. It was on that wall when you sat down in row four and it was on when you said yes, and I have been out to that drive-in four times to ask for it.
...Four times.
Four times. They tell me the programme does not change.
You never said you had been asking.
You would have told me not to. You would have been kind about it and you would have told me not to.
Oh — I am sorry. You have walked straight into the middle of us. We are getting married, and we are not, and both of those are true at once.

topics.label: What picture?
replies: THE LONG WAY BACK. Nineteen fifty-seven, and it is the second feature out at the Starlite.
A man drives home and the road keeps putting the same town in front of him. It is meant to be frightening and we laughed all the way through it.
That is what it is about. Ray says it is the most romantic thing he has ever sat through and I have stopped arguing.

topics.label: I will get it played.
replies: ...You will do what?
He has asked four times.
Then go on. We are not going anywhere. That is rather the trouble with us.

topics.label: They ran your picture.
replies: ...Say that again.
RAY. Ray, come here.
We are going in. Come in with us. You are signing, you have to come in.

topics.label: Congratulations.
replies: Thank you. We met on Tuesday. Everyone says that is too fast and everyone is wrong.

npcs.bio: Getting married in about four minutes and has not stopped smiling.

npcs.name: Ray

lines.text: Nervous?
No. Well. Yes. But the good kind.
She says you are signing as a witness. Do not let her down, she has a list.

topics.label: Four times, Ray?
replies: Five, if you count the night I got as far as the ramp and turned round.
The man in the booth is not unkind about it. He says the programme does not change, and he says it the way you would say the tide does not change.
It is the one thing I have promised her. I would rather stand in this lobby all night than go in there having not done it.

topics.label: It is only a picture.
replies: Everybody says that. Marla says that.
This town does not finish anything. Nobody remembers the street, the monorail does not come, the drinks are free and the night does not end.
I would like one thing to have a last reel. Then I will marry her and I will not ask for anything else.

topics.label: Good luck.
replies: Thank you. Do not tell her about the fifth time.

npcs.bio: Marrying Marla. Has been holding the same bunch of flowers for an hour.

npcs.name: Delacroix

lines.text: Big night?
Every night is the same night at this table. That is rather the point of the table.
Sit if you like. You will not be able to afford the seat, and I am going to enjoy watching you work that out.

topics.label: BIRTHDAY.
replies: Delacroix does not look up from his cards.
“Say it once more and say it quieter.”
He plays the hand out. He plays it badly and he plays it out anyway, because a man who leaves a table in the middle of a hand is a man somebody remembers leaving.
Then he reaches under the felt and puts a shoebox on it: brown paper, string, and a red wafer of wax across the knot with a thumb pressed into it.
“Nine weeks that has been under this table. Nine weeks of a room full of people watching my hands and not one of them watching the floor.”
“Nothing. It is a box. It has been a box for nine weeks and it will go on being a box right up until somebody opens it, and then it will be evidence.”
“Out through the front, and nod at the desk on your way. The lady at the desk is the only person in this building I am afraid of.”

topics.label: They say I own the house across the road.
replies: That is the word on the floor, and the word on the floor is wrong about most things and never about ownership.
It does not make you rich. It makes you responsible, which is the expensive version.
Ask the old man in the good suit who drinks over there. He has an envelope about it and he has never once pretended he has not.

topics.label: What is the eight worth in here?
replies: Nothing at the tables. Everything at the door.
I have watched a man be turned away from this room for a jacket, and I have watched the same room open up for somebody wearing that mark on a cheap chain.
Nobody I could point to. That is what unsettled me. The door was shut and then it was not, and the man who ought to have opened it was looking the other way and stayed looking the other way.

topics.label: Do you ever leave?
replies: I have a flight most weeks. I am extremely good at not being on it.
Do not look at me like that. Half this street has a flight most weeks.

topics.label: Good luck at the table.
replies: Luck is for the other side of the felt. Good evening.

npcs.bio: Plays only at the high table, and has played only at this one for nine weeks. Claims never to have lost, which is how you know he has.

npcs.name: Ruby

lines.text: What is on tonight?
Me, mostly. Doors at eight. Do not sit in the front row unless you like being part of it.
Funny thing. The eight on that sign was there before the casino was. Nobody knows who painted it.

topics.label: You said the eight was there before the casino.
replies: Before the casino, before the road, before the water came out this far. That is not me being poetic, that is what the sign painter's family will tell you and they have the ledgers.
Ines does the repaint. Little woman, ladder, out on the boulevard most mornings. Her grandmother did it before her.
Ask her what happens if she changes it. Go on. Ask her exactly that and watch her face.

topics.label: What is the second act?
replies: Fifteen minutes, one dress, and a light cue at the end that I have hit four thousand times.
On the last bar every lamp in the house swings over to the doors and holds. Audience always turns round. Every night. They cannot help it.
Because that is where the lamps were bolted, love, and nobody has moved a bolt in this building since it went up.
Sit in row nine. Camille will not want to let you and Camille is wrong.

topics.label: See you at eight.
replies: Doors at eight. It is always eight. Do keep up.

npcs.bio: Second act, seven nights a week, and still the best fifteen minutes in town.

npcs.name: Dolores

lines.text: Enjoying yourselves?
We were supposed to leave on Sunday. It is Wednesday. I do not want to talk about it.
Stand still, would you? Harold has never photographed anything like you in his life.

topics.label: Why have you not left?
replies: We try. That is the thing nobody believes and I have stopped telling it to people who have somewhere to be.
Cab to the airport. Every time. And every time we are back on this street with the bags at our feet and Harold saying well, one more night then, and I cannot tell you what happened in between.
Not once. Four days. Or nine. I have stopped counting because the counting was the part that was frightening me.

topics.label: Does anybody else have this problem?
replies: Everybody has this problem. Nobody calls it a problem. They call it Vegas and they laugh.
Ask the woman who changes the letters on the board at the east end how long she has been meaning to hand her notice in.

topics.label: I hope you get home.
replies: You are very kind. Hold still, Harold is coming.

npcs.bio: On day four of a two-day trip. Has a very full camera and no plan whatsoever.

npcs.name: Harold

lines.text: She says you want a picture.
If it is no trouble. Hold the sword up a bit. Lovely. Nobody at home will believe a word of it.
Mind you, nobody at home believes anything I say.

topics.label: Have you looked at any of the photographs?
replies: Once. Rolls and rolls of them, back at the hotel, spread out on the bed because Dolores was asleep and I could not be.
Every one of them is this street. Correct street, correct lights, correct people, and not one of them has anything in it I remembered taking.
It does. It happens to everybody and everybody says so, which I found less comforting than I expected to.

topics.label: Take one of me, then.
replies: Right. Hold the sword up. Lovely. — Hm.
Nothing. The light went funny. Let me do another one.
...There. That is better. I will not look at it tonight.

topics.label: Enjoy your evening.
replies: We will. We always do. That is rather the trouble.

npcs.bio: Married to Dolores. Has taken nine hundred photographs and looked at none of them.

npcs.name: Sam

lines.text: You have not asked why I look like this.
Son, I have been here since before that sign went up. You are not the first.
The first what?
Ask me again some night when the lights go out. They do, you know. All at once, about every eight years.
And the writing on that sign is not English. Never has been. Go on, take a proper look at it.

topics.label: Tell me about the lights going out.
replies: Sixty-eight was the first I marked down. Then seventy-six. Then eighty-four, ninety-two, two thousand, and so on, and you can set your watch by it if you have got eight years to spare.
Whole town. All at once. Not a flicker — off. Eight seconds, near enough, and then everything comes back on doing exactly what it was doing before, including the clocks.
Every one of them. Now you tell me what kind of power cut does that.

topics.label: What is written on the sign, then?
replies: Not English. I traced it with a bit of paper and a pencil when I was nineteen, because a girl bet me I would not.
Two rings. One sat over the other, and the top one smaller. Every line in it is a curve. There is not a straight in the whole mark and that is not how anybody letters a sign.
I know it is, son. I have been looking at it since you walked up and deciding whether I could be bothered to be frightened.
Turns out I cannot. I am eighty-one.

topics.label: You said I am not the first.
replies: Nineteen fifty-seven. I was nine years old and out past where I should have been.

Tall one. Grey, going white at the muzzle. Stood at the end of this street where the paving changes and looked up at the sign for a very long time, the way you look at a thing you were not expecting to still be there.
Come the morning nobody could agree he had been there. Not argued about it — could not agree. Same as if you asked four people what they dreamt.
But he is still here. He never left. You have walked past him twice already and you were too polite to stare.

topics.label: I should let you get on.
replies: Take your time. Nobody here is going anywhere, and I mean that more literally than you would like.

npcs.bio: Has lived here longer than the sign has. Does not appear to find any of this unusual.

npcs.name: Gina

lines.text: What is on tonight?
The same thing.
It has said the same thing since the day I got the job. I still come and change it. They still pay me. I have stopped asking.

topics.label: What does the board say?
replies: Two columns. TONIGHT and NEXT WEEK. The tonight column has a picture in it.
Blank. Sixty years of blank. I have got a box of letters for a column that has never once been filled in and I stand under it eight hours a day.
Say it out loud like that and it does sound like something, does it not. I try not to say it out loud.

topics.label: What is the board bolted to?
replies: A plate. It was there before the board and the board was put up over it, and there is lettering on the plate — painted over twice and you can still read it in a low sun.
It is not a word. It is that mark of yours. Two rings, one over the other, about a foot across, and somebody has gone to the trouble of painting over it twice.

topics.label: Have you been out there?
replies: To the Starlite? I put the letters up for it. I have never driven out and sat in front of it.
...I could not tell you. It is two miles. I have said "one of these nights" for longer than I have had this job, and I have said it in the same tone every time, which I did not notice until just now.
If you are going out there, look at the board on the way past. Tell me whether the next-week column is still empty. I would rather hear it from somebody who has only looked at it once.

topics.label: I will let you get back to it.
replies: Back to what? — sorry. That was unkind and it was not aimed at you. Mind the step, it is not level either.

npcs.bio: Changes the letters on the Starlite board at the east end of the street. The picture has not changed since before she started.

npcs.name: Cass

lines.text: That is a good voice.
It is a loud voice. In this street that is the same thing.
Stick around for the top of the hour. The whole ceiling goes off and everybody looks up like it is the first time.

topics.label: Tell me about the ceiling.
replies: Eight minutes long, top of every hour, and I have been under it six nights a week for eleven years, so call it four thousand.
There is a frame in it that is not in it.
Meaning about two thirds through, right where the horses turn, there is a single frame of something else. You cannot see it. You feel it, the way you feel somebody has come in behind you.
I filmed it on my phone. Went through it one frame at a time in a diner at four in the morning like a lunatic.
It is a ring. Two rings. One over the other, filling the whole ceiling, and it is there for one frame in eight minutes and it has been in that reel since before the reel was digital.

topics.label: Have you told anybody?
replies: I told the engineer. He was very kind about it.
He also went and checked, and he came back the next night and did not want to talk about it, and he has not looked me in the eye since. Make of that what you like.

topics.label: Where could I see it properly?
replies: On something bigger than a ceiling, is where. That thing is eight feet over your head and it is gone before you have finished looking up.
East. Out past the square, on the highway — the Starlite. Sixty foot of wall and a man up in the box who has been running the same programme since before I was born.
Roy. Ask him about reel three and then watch his face, because I asked him once at a funeral and he put his drink down.
...If you do get him to run it, do me one kindness. Look at the whole of it. I have had eleven years of the corner of my eye.

topics.label: Sing something for me.
replies: For you? Go on then. — you will want to be somewhere else by the top of the hour, though. Everybody looks up and nobody looks at where they are standing.

npcs.bio: Sings under the canopy six nights a week and out-earns most of the casinos on the block.

npcs.name: Otis

lines.text: What is all this out here?
The boneyard. Every sign this town ever switched off. I keep them lit in my head.
There is one at the back I cannot read. Been here longer than the rest. Curly writing, sort of. Looks like a figure eight lying down.
Can I see it?
Help yourself. Nobody else has ever asked.

topics.label: You have got some of them lit.
replies: He does not look up. He has been looking at them for fifty years and he does not need to.
"Some. All of them some." He says it like a man correcting a figure rather than a man being modest.

"You do not do a sign. You do a tube. There are four hundred and ten tubes on this lot and I have got a hundred and sixty of them back, and the rest of it is a question of glass and time and I have plenty of one of those."
"WISHING WELL. Off since 1955, which is longer than any of them, so it is furthest back in the queue and it is also the one I would do first if I was a sentimental man."

"SUNSET LANES came in last and it lights nearly all the way. That is not me. That is it being newer. People will tell you a sign that has been out thirty years and a sign that has been out sixty are the same sign. They are not the same sign."
"I will have the lot of them going. Not soon. But I will have them."
"It is not a boneyard if things leave it working." He looks at the board for the first time since he hung it. "Nothing has left it yet. But it is not a boneyard."

topics.label: Has anybody dropped anything out here?
replies: "Constantly. It is a field of dead signs with no gate on it."
"There is a wallet under the WISHING WELL. Has been since Tuesday."
"I do not go into that building and that building does not come out here, and we have had forty years of a very good arrangement."
"You take it. You look like somebody who is allowed in."

topics.label: Take me to the one you cannot read.
replies: Back row, on its face, under the tarp. Been there since before I was keeping the place and I have been keeping the place since seventy-four.
Now. I have hung nine hundred signs in my life, and I want to tell you four things about that one.
It has no fixings. No bolt holes, no lugs, nothing to hang it by.
It has no lamp housings and no wiring, so it never lit and was never meant to.
It is not steel and it is not aluminium and it is not any plastic I have ever cut.
And it is a ring. A whole round ring, sawn clean through in two places, laid down flat.
No. It is not. I have known that for fifty years and you are the first person to be told, because you are the first person to ask me twice.

topics.label: Where did it come from?
replies: Bought as scrap, fifty-seven, off a fella clearing a lot out on the highway. Paid by weight. I have got the docket.
The lot is that fenced-off square out past the diner. There was nothing on it then and there is a fence round it now, and I would like somebody to explain to me which of those is the strange one.

topics.label: Can it be turned over?
replies: Six men and a crane, nineteen eighty-eight. Crane lifted the truck off its wheels and the ring did not come up.
Same crane took a forty-foot cowboy off that corner the week before.
That is the question, is it not. Because in ninety-one two lads moved it eight feet on a sack barrow for a laugh, and I saw them do it.
It weighs what it wants to weigh. That is not a sensible thing for a man of my age to say and I am saying it anyway.

topics.label: You said a crane took the cowboy down.
replies: It did. Nineteen eighty-eight, the week before we tried the ring. I was there. I held the tag line.
I know.
I have known for thirty-seven years. I walk under him twice a day and I have never once looked up on purpose, and I would ask you not to make a thing of it.
Yard in Henderson. I signed the docket. I have got the docket in the same drawer as the other docket, which is a sentence I have never said out loud before and do not care for.
He still says it, you know. Every quarter of an hour, same as he always did. There is nobody paying the power on that corner. I checked. I have checked twice.

topics.label: Have you been dreaming about a fox?
replies: ...Say that again.
Forty years I have been out here and the only person I ever told was him, and he turned up two weeks later and asked me the same question you just did.
Every night since they took the cowboy down. She is in a box and she is asking, and I do not speak whatever she is asking IN, and I know exactly what she is saying.

topics.label: What do you know about the base up north?
replies: I know what everybody knows and one thing they do not.

Trucks. Twelve go in on a Tuesday and eleven come out on the Thursday, and I have counted them from this yard for nineteen years because from here you can see the road and nobody thinks a man in a scrapyard is counting anything.
The twelfth truck has never come back out. Not once. Not one of them, in nineteen years, and I would like somebody to tell me what a base does with nine hundred trucks.

topics.label: Thank you, Otis.
replies: Do not thank me. Come back and tell me what it is. I would like to know before I go, and I am not being morbid, I am being seventy-nine.

npcs.bio: Keeps the boneyard. Knows the name of every dead sign in it and will tell you all of them.

npcs.name: Nadia

lines.text: How is your night going?
I am up four hundred.
Do not ask me since when.

topics.label: How is it going tonight?
replies: Up four hundred. Four hundred and twenty, if we are counting the first table, and we are.
Before that is not tonight.
You want the number. Everybody wants the number. Two thousand. There. Now we have both got it and neither of us is any better off.

topics.label: Do you always play here?
replies: Six nights. Not seven — I am not an animal.
The seventh I sit at home and I do the arithmetic properly, on paper, and it comes out the way it comes out, and then it is Monday and the arithmetic was done by somebody else.

topics.label: What keeps you at it?
replies: The hand before last. Always the hand before last. Never the one coming.
I know it is backwards. I have known it was backwards for a long time. It has never once helped to know it.

Look up, though. Go on. — everybody looks up here and forgets what they were about to say, and I have watched it happen four hundred times, and it has happened to me and I could not tell you what I was about to say either.

topics.label: Good luck.
replies: Luck is the part I have got plenty of. It is the leaving I am no good at.

npcs.bio: Up four hundred, which she will explain at length, and down two thousand, which she will not.

npcs.name: Whitfield

lines.text: Busy night?
Forty-one thousand people came down this street today. Tomorrow it will be forty-three.
And not one of them will remember a single thing about it. Marvellous business.

topics.label: Do the numbers work out?
replies: No.
I count arrivals at four gates, three stations and eleven hotels. I count departures the same way. I have done it for nine years and the two numbers have never once agreed.
It is a small gap. Fractions of a per cent. On forty thousand a day a small gap is a coach party.
More people arrive than leave. Every day. For nine years.
And before you say it — no, the hotels are not full. I check the hotels. That is the part I do not put in the report.

topics.label: What do you put in the report?
replies: Forty-one thousand. Rounded. A footnote about measurement error which I wrote once in twenty-nineteen and have pasted in every quarter since.
I am not a coward. I am a woman with a mortgage and a very specific set of skills that are worth nothing anywhere else.

topics.label: Good night.
replies: Forty-three thousand tomorrow. Or thereabouts. Good night.

npcs.bio: Somebody important at somewhere important. Talks entirely in numbers.

npcs.name: June

lines.text: Table for one?
Sit anywhere, hon. Coffee is on.
You want my advice, do not go poking round that gate up the road. The men out there do not wear names.
What is behind it?
Nothing. That is the official position and I would not go arguing with it in daylight.

topics.label: Tell me about the men from the gate.
replies: In on a Thursday, four of them, same booth, and I could not tell you one thing about a single face.
They order. Every time. Full breakfast, four of them, and it goes back cold and untouched and they pay in cash and they tip properly.
Nobody eats, hon. Twenty-six years I have been carrying plates and you learn to read a table, and that table reads like four people doing an impression of four people.

topics.label: What is really behind that fence?
replies: Officially nothing, and I said I would not argue with that in daylight, and it is dark now, so.
There is a ramp. You can see the top of it from the ridge behind the gas station. A ramp goes down, and a thing you build a ramp down to is a thing that is underneath.

topics.label: Coffee, then.
replies: Sit anywhere. And listen — if you are going up that road tonight, eat something first. That is not folklore, that is a waitress.

npcs.bio: Works the counter at the diner out on the highway. Has seen absolutely everything come through that door.

npcs.name: Wade

lines.text: Long way out here.
Four hundred miles of nothing and then all of that behind you. I prefer the nothing.
See lights out over the flats most weeks. Used to phone it in. Nobody ever came, so I quit phoning.

topics.label: What is wrong with the road?
replies: Nothing is wrong with the road. The road is fine. It is the distance that is wrong.

Town to the state line and back is two hundred and eighteen miles. Been driving it eighteen years. Some nights the odometer says two hundred and eighteen and some nights it says two hundred and ten, and I am not the man who takes a shortcut across a desert.
Every eight years or so it is a big one. Other times it is a mile or two. I have a notebook. I have never shown it to anybody and I am not going to start with somebody wearing that.

topics.label: The lights over the flats.
replies: Low, slow, no sound, and they do not have the decency to be in a formation so a man could feel silly about it.
They sit over that fenced square. Not above it — on it. Come down and stop about the height of a house and go out.
Phoned it in four times in the eighties. Nobody came. The fifth time I did not phone and somebody came anyway and knocked on my cab at three in the morning to ask if I had seen anything.

topics.label: Safe roads.
replies: You too. Whatever it is you are driving.

npcs.bio: Drives the long haul across the desert and has stopped being startled by lights in the sky.

npcs.name: Dr Alma Reyes

lines.text: What brings you out here?
Geology.
That is a lot of equipment for geology.
It is very interesting geology.
...We logged a signal out of that gate in sixty-eight. Eight pulses, then quiet. Every eight years since, to the day.
You have got an eight on your chest. I am going to go and sit down for a minute.

topics.label: Tell me about the eight pulses.
replies: Fourteenth of October, nineteen sixty-eight. Eight pulses out of that compound, evenly spaced, one point one seconds apart, and then nothing for eight years.

Fourteenth of October, seventy-six. Same eight. Eighty-four, ninety-two, two thousand, and on, and on, to the day, and I have the tape for every one of them since ninety-two because I have been sitting in a folding chair in a desert for most of my adult life.
That is the whole of my career, that question. And the answer is that the next one is due, and it is close, and I am out here in October with a chair.

topics.label: What happens in town when it fires?
replies: Every light in the county goes out for eight seconds.
The power company files it as a fault and has filed it as a fault six times without ever finding one. The town calls it the Blink and thinks it is charming.
I have. Twice, in writing, to people who are paid to read things.
It is not that they disbelieved me. It is that they read it, and agreed, and then went to lunch, and it never came up again. This town is very good at that.

topics.label: What do you think it is?
replies: A door with the power off, knocking once every eight years to see if anybody is still on the other side.
I have never said that sentence out loud before. I would like you to know it cost me something.

topics.label: I will let you get back to your rocks.
replies: It really is very interesting geology. — no, it is not. Go and talk to Roxy. She has been inside and I have not, and it has been eating me for eleven years.

npcs.bio: Says she studies rocks. Is standing a very long way from any interesting rocks.

npcs.name: Frankie

lines.text: Deal me in?
Table minimum is more than you are carrying, friend, and I can tell that from here.
Tell you what. Sit down anyway. Owner drinks free, and there is an argument on this floor about who that is, and I have money on you.

topics.label: Does the house ever lose?
replies: The house loses all night. The house is very relaxed about it.
There is one table it does not lose at and it is not one of the money ones. It is the eight in the carpet, back of the floor, and nobody deals on it because there is no table on it.

topics.label: What is the eight in the carpet?
replies: Pattern. Woven in. Re-woven five times that I know of because carpet wears, and every time it comes back identical.
The order goes to the mill with a line on it that says PATTERN PER CONTRACT DO NOT VARY, and no one has ever seen the contract.

topics.label: Deal them out, Frankie.
replies: On the house. Which is you. Which never stops being funny.

npcs.bio: Deals blackjack at the near table. Fastest hands on the floor and the worst jokes.

npcs.name: Lena

lines.text: Anything good?
Everything is free and everything is watered. That is the arrangement.
You are the first customer in nine years to say thank you. I am putting that in my book.

topics.label: Did you see Ryan leave?
replies: ...Put your hand on the tray. Like you are taking a drink off it. There. Now we are two people having a nothing.
Four of them. Black suits, and not the good kind — the kind that all came out of the same shop on the same afternoon.
They did not walk him out. They put him in the trunk of a black car on the north side, and the car went up the boulevard and then it turned east, out towards the desert.
Nine years I have carried this tray and I have two hundred and eleven names in my book, and not one of them looked up.
I was never here. I said nothing.
And love — you put your own name in the book when you get back.

topics.label: Why is everything free?
replies: Because it does not go anywhere.
Meaning I have carried this tray for nine years and I have never once taken money for anything on it, and the bar stock does not go down, and I have stopped mentioning it at the staff meeting.
Whatever you have got in your pocket, love — it is not going to spend here. Not because you are not welcome. Because it is not here either.

topics.label: What is in your book?
replies: Everyone who says thank you. Nine years, two hundred and eleven names.
You are two hundred and twelve, and you are the first one I have had to draw.

topics.label: Thank you, Lena.
replies: ...Two hundred and thirteen. Go on with you.

npcs.bio: Works the floor with a tray and has never once dropped it.

npcs.name: Mr Halloran

lines.text: Quiet tonight.
It is never quiet. It is only ever slow.
I have got your face on eleven cameras and not one of them likes it. Take that as a compliment, most faces get twelve.

topics.label: BIRTHDAY.
replies: Mr Halloran does not move.
“Say that again.”
He looks at you for four full seconds and eleven cameras look at the two of you.
“No.”
“I have known that word for thirty years and I have never once had to use it, and I would like to keep the run going.”
“Nothing of that kind happens in this building. Not on my floor, not in my drawers, not for nine weeks while I look the other way.”
“And that is not me being a good man. That is Mr Win, and Mr Win has been extremely clear about it for longer than I have worked here.”
“Across the boulevard. The Pyramid runs a high table and there is a man sitting at it who has not stood up in nine weeks.”
“Go and be somebody else’s problem. Smile at the door on the way out.”

topics.label: I am looking for Ryan.
replies: Ryan the Magnificent.
He is not on the floor.
He was extended credit. He did not retire it. That is the whole of it, and it is the whole of it every time.
Eleven cameras and I did not need one of them. Third table from the door, nine hours, and a man doing arithmetic he had already finished about six hours previously.
So the house asked him to settle. He could not. So the house asked him to leave, and he left.
Before your show. Which I know about, because everybody knows about it. Vito has been on the telephone all evening and Vito does not use the telephone.
And that is where my part of it ends. I run a floor. What happens on the boulevard is the boulevard’s.

topics.label: Vince says you keep the paper.
replies: Vince talks.
...Vince is right.

Bottom drawer, under the float sheets, in an envelope that has been opened once. Nineteen sixty-one. Previous holder signs the whole thing over and the line where the new name goes says, in his hand: THE NEXT ONE THROUGH THE DOOR.
No, it is not, and it has held for sixty-five years against four sets of lawyers, and I have stopped enquiring into why.

topics.label: Who signed it over?
replies: No name. A mark.

Two rings, one over the other, done in one movement without lifting the pen — and I know it was one movement because I have looked at that signature under a glass more times than I would care to put in a sentence.
Left the building at four in the morning, walked north up the boulevard, and that is the end of everything anybody has.
He did not leave town, though. I want to be careful here. He never left town.

topics.label: Why have you kept it?
replies: Because somebody had to, and because for forty years I have been the only person in this building who thought the envelope was real.
You want it? It is yours. It has always been yours, apparently. I would take it as a personal kindness if you did not change the carpet.

topics.label: Not tonight, Mr Halloran.
replies: It will be in the drawer. It is very good at being in the drawer.

npcs.bio: Pit boss. Watches everything at once and never appears to be watching anything.

npcs.name: Reverend Bo

lines.text: Do you need paperwork?
I need two of you and about ninety seconds. Do you have two of you?
No? Then sit at the back and enjoy the next one. There is always a next one.

topics.label: Marla asked me to witness.
replies: Then you are wanted, and you are wanted in about four minutes, and you will want to know what you are signing.
Two lines. Names of the couple, names of the witnesses, and the date. That is the whole of it and it is the most binding thing in this town.
It stays. Everything else here goes — the money, the night, what people can remember of it. The book stays.
Faye keeps the book. Talk to Faye before you sign. She will want a look at you and she has earned it.

topics.label: Nine thousand couples.
replies: Nine thousand and some. I cried at forty.
I could not tell you which forty. Every one of them was the same ninety seconds and every one of them was not, and if you can hold both of those at once you can do this job.

topics.label: What do you need from me?
replies: Two of them. Any two of them, and about ninety seconds.
Look at them. Eleven people came in here tonight on their own and nine thousand couples have come in here together, and I have never once been able to do anything about the first number.
Then Peggy will tell you. She tells everybody. She has been telling me for thirty years and she has been right for thirty years and I have never asked her how.
Go and sit with them. All of them. They will tell you what they are after and they will tell you what they have noticed, and the second one is worth more than the first one.

topics.label: The tin.
replies: He turns the collection tin upside down on the front pew and does not count it, which after nine thousand weddings is a decision and not an oversight.
Four of them left what they left. It is yours. I did the ninety seconds, you did the eleven years.
It took THEM eleven years. Take the money.

topics.label: Marla and Ray are coming in.
replies: Are they now.
They are all stuck on something. That is what the pews are for.
Two of them, and they arrived AS two. Do you know how long it has been since somebody walked in here already holding somebody's hand?
Go and see Faye. She keeps the book and she will want a look at you first, and she has earned it.

topics.label: I will sit at the back.
replies: There is always a next one. Usually within the hour.

npcs.bio: Has married nine thousand couples and cried at roughly forty of them.

npcs.name: Peggy

lines.text: Nice organ.
It is a terrible organ. Two of the keys go nowhere and one of them screams.
I have played it so long I can hear which couples will last. Not many. Yours might.

topics.label: Which key screams?
replies: C sharp, second octave. Has done since they put the organ in and the man who tuned it said there was nothing wrong with it, which there is not.
It is not the organ. The organ is in tune. It is that the note is already in the room and the key just joins it.
Under everything. All the time. You cannot hear it, you can only hear when something agrees with it.
Hold your hand flat on the wall of the big building up the road with the light on top. Go on. Then come back and press this key and tell me they are not the same thing.

topics.label: Has anyone else noticed?
replies: Forty-one years and one man, and he was drunk and he was leaving.
And now you, and you are neither, which is the best evening I have had in a while.

topics.label: Can you really hear it?
replies: I can hear four bars of it. That is all anybody gets.
It is not magic and it is not kindness, love, it is that I have played the same four bars at nine thousand of these and I have watched what walks up that aisle while I am playing them.
I can tell when it is WRONG. That is a different thing and it is the only thing I have ever been sure of. Being sure it is right is the couple’s job and they are welcome to it.

topics.label: Which two should it be?
replies: Four for four and not one of them mine.
I have played that organ for thirty-one years waiting for a night where somebody in the room was doing the same job I am doing, and you have gone and done it in an hour in a coat.
Go on. Faye has the pen out.

topics.label: Play me out, Peggy.
replies: Four bars. It is always four bars. Off you go.

npcs.bio: Plays the same four bars nine hundred times a week and has made peace with it.

npcs.name: Vito

lines.text: Sorry the show is delayed! The magician has been missing, he is our opening act, and the crowd is getting restless.
Four hundred people who have paid, and a stage with nobody on it. You can hear it starting. That noise they make.

topics.label: What are the magic tricks? How does it work?
replies: Three tricks. One button. That is the whole act.
THE TRUNK. A tumbler runs along the barrel. Press it in the green. Three pins, and the green gets smaller.
THE HAT. A dove flies a circle. Let it go when it is pointing at a lamp that is still dark. Four lamps, eight doves.
THE LAST CUE. Every lamp in the house swings to the doors. Hand up the moment they get there. One press.
Then you got it wrong in front of four hundred people and I go on early. Nobody has ever died of it. Not in here.

topics.label: Who is the magician?
replies: RYAN THE MAGNIFICENT. Nineteen years on that stage and the name was already too big for him when he got it.
He gambles. That is not gossip, that is a timetable — you can set a watch by which room he is in.
So he is at big WIN casino. He is always at big WIN casino.
Then he is somewhere worse and it is still Tuesday, and I have got a crowd out there.
His trunk is on my stage and his car is out the front with the doors shut, and the doors on that car do not shut on their own. You can make of that whatever you like. I have got a show.

topics.label: Who are you?
replies: Vito. I sing at twenty past.
I also book the openers, pay the band, count the house and go out there and tell four hundred people when a man has not turned up. Manager is not a job here, kid. It is what is left over.
Fifty years I have had this room, and I have never once had it to myself.

topics.label: What is this place?
replies: The Showroom. Four hundred seats, one door, and a ceiling that has not been switched off since they put it in.
Everything else on this street is built to keep you walking. This is the one room in town built to make you sit down and look one way.
And it is very good at it. Whether that is the room or the town I stopped asking about forty years ago.

topics.label: You asked about the eight once.
replies: A long time ago and a very long drink ago, and the fella who booked the room said the eight came with the building and looked at me like I had asked him what colour the air was.
So I dropped it. That is what you do at that age. You want the room more than you want the answer.
Now I have had the room for fifty years and I would quite like the answer, and here you are with it painted on your chest, and I am on in twenty minutes.
Life is like that. Mostly it is like that.

topics.label: Why is it always eight?
replies: Doors at eight, curtain at eight, and the sign says EIGHT in letters four foot high, and there is no eight o'clock show. Curtain is twenty past.
Twenty past. For fifty years. Nobody has ever fixed the sign and nobody has ever complained, and that is not a town being lazy, kid. That is a town not being allowed.

topics.label: Break a leg.
replies: Every night is a big night. Sit down the front, I will find you.

npcs.bio: Headlines the room and runs it, which in a house this size is one job. Has not changed the set list since the room opened and will not be asked to.

npcs.name: Camille

lines.text: Any seat going?
Row nine. Do not argue with me, everybody argues with me and nobody wins.
Row nine is the best seat in the room anyway. I keep that to myself.

topics.label: Why is row nine the best seat?
replies: Because it is the only row that is straight on to the doors, and the doors are what the last light cue swings to.
From row nine at the end of the second act you are looking straight down the beam of every lamp in this house, out through the doors, up the boulevard.
At the light on top of the Pyramid. Dead on. Every night, for about four seconds, and then the house comes up and everybody claps.
I have sat in nine on my night off to check, because I am the sort of person who checks.

topics.label: Has anybody built this on purpose?
replies: The lamps were bolted in nineteen sixty-two and the Pyramid went up in ninety-three.
So either that is the luckiest bolt-hole in Nevada, or somebody knew in sixty-two where they were going to put a building thirty years later.
I would like it to be luck. It is not, though, is it.

topics.label: Row nine it is.
replies: Do not argue with me. Nobody wins. Enjoy the show.

npcs.bio: Seats the room, and will absolutely not let you sit closer than your ticket says.

npcs.name: Nathan

lines.text: What is the light for?
Tourism, officially.
Off the record, it points at nothing. We checked. There is nothing up there at all, which is a very strange thing to build a building at.

topics.label: What is the one true fact in the tour?
replies: That the beam is on a separate supply. Everything else in the tour is either rounded, invented or lifted off a postcard.
Its own feed, its own plant, and its own generators in the basement, which is a great deal of trouble to go to for a light.
It is the only thing in this county that stays on when the town goes dark. I have been up here for one of those. Whole valley out and this thing going straight up like nothing had happened.

topics.label: You said it points at nothing.
replies: We had it checked in twenty-fourteen because a guest complained, which is the only reason anything ever gets checked.
Nothing at the far end. No station, no satellite, nothing catalogued on that bearing at any altitude.
The report says NO TERMINUS IDENTIFIED and I have thought about those two words a great deal more than the man who typed them.

topics.label: Enjoy the rest of the tour.
replies: Nine minutes. It goes quickly. Most things here do.

npcs.bio: Guides the tour, which is nine minutes long and contains one true fact.

npcs.name: Estelle

lines.text: What is downstairs?
Nothing anybody wants to look at. Pottery, mostly. And one piece we cannot place.
It is a chest plate. Eight worked into the front of it, two rings, one over the other. Came out of the sand about a mile from here.
...You are wearing it. Would you mind sitting down and starting from the beginning?

topics.label: Show me the chest plate.
replies: It is downstairs, and you are the first person in nine years to say yes, and I am going to walk very fast so do keep up.
There. Two rings, one over the other, worked into the front. The top one smaller. And it is not decoration, it is a fitting — there are lugs on the back of it.
For fixing it to something. It is not armour. It is a plate off a machine, and somebody has worn it since, because the edges are rounded where a strap has been.
You are wearing the same mark and I would very much like to sit down, and I would very much like you not to leave.

topics.label: Where exactly did it come from?
replies: Sand, about a mile east. Nineteen seventy-one, road crew, and it came to us because nobody could think of anywhere else to send it.
A mile east is the fenced square. I have said that to the board twice and both times it went into the minutes as an aside.

topics.label: What else is down there?
replies: Pottery. Genuinely pottery. I was not being modest, it is almost all pottery.
And a box of photographs of the site before the fence, which I am not supposed to have, and which I will show to a person who asks me about the plate first. You asked about the plate first.

topics.label: I will come back for the rest.
replies: Do. Please do. I will be here — everyone is always here, have you noticed that? — I will be here.

npcs.bio: Keeps the collection downstairs. Very keen to show somebody, anybody, the collection downstairs.

npcs.name: Mayor Mr. Win

lines.text: You are the mayor?
I am. Before that I built. Fifty years of putting up rooms in a town that had none worth standing in.
And this is the one room I did not put up. I bought it. There is a difference and it took me twenty years to feel it.

topics.label: This house has your name on it.
replies: The house had the name first. I have been Mr Win since I was nine years old and my mother had a fresh opinion about it every day of her life.
When it came up for sale I stood on that pavement and read the sign and thought: well. There is no arguing with that.

topics.label: Nothing crooked happens in here.
replies: No. And I would like to be exact about it, because people are generous about it and they should not be.
It is not that my people are better than anybody else’s. It is that there is one rule, and it is old, and it is short: no business in my house that is not the house’s business.
Thirty years. Halloran keeps it, Lena keeps it, and the last man who tested it is still in this town and still will not come through that door.
You can lose every dollar you own at that table. You will not lose anything else, nobody will lend you a cent, and nobody will follow you out.

topics.label: There is a paper in Halloran’s drawer with no name on it.
replies: There is. Nineteen sixty-one, and the line where the owner goes says THE NEXT ONE THROUGH THE DOOR, in a hand nobody has ever put a name to.
I bought this building in ninety-four and that envelope came with it. My lawyers spent four months telling me it was worthless and I have kept it in the safe every day since.
Because I did not buy the door. I bought the walls and the licence and the carpet. Somebody a long way before me gave the door away.
One day somebody is going to come through it, and it is going to be a very short conversation, and I intend to have it politely.
...You have been in and out of that door six times tonight. I have counted.

topics.label: I put my hand on the mark under the Pyramid.
replies: ...And?
Cut. Yes. I have said that to three engineers and every one of them told me it was cast, because cast is what a thing like that ought to be, and none of them had put their hand on it.
Thank you. That is not a small thing you have just done for me.

topics.label: Who chose where to put the Pyramid?
replies: I did not. That is the answer and it has embarrassed me for thirty years.

I was building on the north end. Good site, good money, drawings done. And a man came to my office with a survey and a cheque and a condition, and the condition was the footprint. Not the height, not the shape, not the light. The footprint. To the inch.
I have his card. It is a very good card and there is nothing on it that is true. I checked all of it eventually, the way you do at three in the morning about ten years too late.
The mark was already in the ground. We poured around it. I remember thinking somebody ought to write that down, and nobody did, and now I am ninety and telling a fox.

topics.label: What is the beam for?
replies: Officially it is the largest of its kind and it can be seen from orbit, which is the sort of sentence you commission when you do not know the answer.

Marisol runs it nights. Engineer. She has measured that beam and she will tell you a thing about it that I did not want to hear, and then I heard it, and then I built a garden on the roof so I would have a reason to go up there.

topics.label: Thank you, Mr Win.
replies: No. Thank you. I go across that boulevard most nights to stand in the best room I ever built, waiting for somebody to notice what it is standing on. Tonight somebody did.

npcs.bio: Built half of what you walked past to get here, then got elected to run the rest of it. Owns this house, and has kept one rule in it for thirty years.

npcs.name: Sonny Vega

lines.text: Good room tonight?
Every room is a good room if you work it right, kid.
How long have you played here?
Longer than the carpet. Longer than the sign. Ask me how long and watch me change the subject.
Lovely weather. See?
...I will tell you one thing for nothing. The eight over that door was here before the door was.

topics.label: How long have you played this room? Really.
replies: I said watch me change the subject. Lovely weather.
I do not know.
I know the room. I know every name on the floor and I know which of them are drinking. I could tell you the set list backwards.

I could not tell you a year. Not one. I have a photograph of myself on that wall in a jacket I do not remember owning and there is no date on it and I have never once thought to ask why there is no date on it until this exact minute, talking to you.

topics.label: Does that frighten you?
replies: It should. It is not going to, because in about four minutes I am going on and I will be fine, and that is the arrangement I have come to.
Everybody in this town has come to that arrangement, kid. You are just the first one to make me say it out loud.

topics.label: Have a good set.
replies: Every room is a good room if you work it right. — and hey. Come back through some time. I would like to find out if I remember you.

npcs.bio: Headlines the big WIN casino lounge and has done since before anyone can remember. Knows every name on the floor and gives none of them away.

npcs.name: Roxy Calderon

lines.text: You have been through the gate.
I have been through a gate. They moved it afterwards, so technically I am a liar and technically I am fine with that.
What was on the other side?
A room. Round. Ring in the floor with lights in it, dead as a doornail for sixty years.
And an eight. Two rings, one over the other, worn nearly flat.
You have got it on your chest, so either you are the best-dressed hoax in Nevada or I am about to have a very good week.

topics.label: Describe the room again. All of it.
replies: Round. Call it seventy feet across, dug down, walls cut not built.
Ring set into the floor, flat, wide as a road. Eight sockets round the inside of it, evenly spaced, and something in each socket that was a lamp once and has not been a lamp for a very long time.
Dead centre, worn down to nearly nothing by boots: your eight. Two rings, one over the other.
Four minutes. Then two men who do not wear names walked me out, and neither of them asked my name either, which I have thought about a great deal since.

topics.label: You said they moved it afterwards.
replies: That is what I was told and I repeated it for six years like an idiot.
They did not move it. You cannot move it. I have flown over that square four hundred times and there is nothing in or out of it bigger than a pickup, ever.
They built over the other end of it.

Hour before sunset, third week of October, the shadow of that fence and the shadow of the Pyramid lie down on one line. I have photographed it from four thousand feet. It is not a coincidence, it is a survey.

topics.label: Is there a way in?
replies: South fence, ring road, where the wire is newer than the posts. That is where they take the trucks down.
I am not going to tell you not to. I would think less of both of us.
But you should know there is nothing living in there, and there are things in there, and I could not make those two sentences agree the whole flight home.

topics.label: Fly safe, Roxy.
replies: If you get inside and there is still an eight on the floor — you come back and you tell me. I have waited eleven years to be told I am not a liar.

npcs.bio: Flies the survey runs over the flats. The only person in the state who has been through that gate and come back out talking, which is why nobody at the gate will look at her.

npcs.name: Sal

lines.text: Keep walking, son.
No. No, you would not, would you. Nobody ever does.
Sixty-nine years I have stood on this corner and not one soul has stopped, and the one that does is wearing the mark.
Sal. That is what they call me here and it has been long enough that it is my name now.

topics.label: You came through the gate.
replies: Fourteenth of October, fifty-seven. Eight seconds, and I was standing in a round room with a ring in the floor and the lights going out one after another like somebody walking away down a corridor.
By the time I got up the ramp it was dark and it has been dark ever since.
Because it will not open, and I have had a lifetime to work out why, and I have.

topics.label: Then tell me why it will not open.
replies: A gate is two pieces. The socket, which is the ring in the floor — that is fixed, that is the hard part, and it is still down there.
And the collar. Goes round it, sits proud of the floor, and it is what actually holds the door. Without it the socket can knock and it cannot open.
Sawn in half and sold for scrap by weight in the spring of fifty-seven, six months before I arrived, to a sign man in this town who thought he was buying a blank.
It is lying face down in his boneyard on Fremont with a tarp over it, and I have stood next to it, and I could not lift a corner of it, and I am not a small fox.

topics.label: What are the eight seconds?
replies: The socket asking. Every eight years, to the day, it draws everything it can reach — takes the whole county with it — and it knocks eight times to see if there is anybody left on the other side to answer.
Nothing solid comes through a gate that cannot open. Only what is not solid.
Meaning look at your hands, son, and then look at that street, and then tell me how you got here.
You are asleep. Somewhere a very long way from this you are asleep, and when you wake up you will have this the way a man has a dream — sure of it, and unable to prove one inch of it.
Same as me. Except I did it once and I never woke up.

topics.label: How do I leave a mark, then?
replies: You cannot. Not on the town. It does not hold — you have seen it, everybody here is halfway through something they cannot finish and none of them can tell you why.
One thing holds. Ink on paper, in a book that is kept, signed by a hand.

There is a chapel on this street with a register going back to the fifties and a woman behind the desk who has never lost a page of it. My name is in that book. Fifty-seven, witness, and a mark instead of a signature because I could not write your letters yet.
It is still there. I have checked it every year for sixty-nine years and it is the only proof I exist.

Then when your ships finally come looking — and they will, they always do, that is the one thing about foxes I would bet a lung on — there will be one line on this whole planet that tells them somebody got here first and where to dig.

topics.label: I will come back, Sal.
replies: They all say that. You might mean it.
Go on. And listen — do not let them see you be surprised by anything. That is the whole trick. Nobody in this town has ever once been surprised and it is the only reason I am still standing here.

npcs.bio: Runs the souvenir cart at the east end of the boulevard. Everyone on this street thinks the suit is a bit. He has let them think it since nineteen fifty-seven.

npcs.name: Ines Salazar

lines.text: You paint the sign?
I paint the eight. Somebody else does the letters, and I have opinions about the letters that nobody has asked for.
Grandmother, mother, me. Same brush width, same two coats, same eight.

topics.label: What happens if you change it?
replies: I do not know, and I want to be honest with you about how much that bothers me.
There is a line in the contract. Not the shape, not the size, not the colour — the SEQUENCE. Outer ring first, anticlockwise, then the inner, clockwise, and they must not meet.
My grandmother let them meet. Nineteen seventy-six, one wet morning, a slip about that long.
She came down the ladder, went home, and did not paint again. She was fifty-one and she lived to be ninety and she never once said why.

topics.label: Who holds the contract?
replies: It comes with the property and the property has been sold four times, and every buyer has signed it without reading it because it is one page and it costs them nothing.
It is not a maintenance clause. I have read a lot of maintenance clauses. It is an instruction.

topics.label: It is on my chest.
replies: Turn to the light. — the inner ring is smaller. Everyone gets that wrong. Every knock-off on this street has them the same size and it makes me want to lie down in the road.
Yours is right. Yours is the first right one I have ever seen that was not painted by my family.
I am going to go and sit on my ladder for a minute, and then I am going to come back and ask you about a hundred things, so do not vanish.

topics.label: I will let you paint.
replies: Two coats. It is always two coats. Mind the tin.

npcs.bio: Third generation on the same ladder. Repaints the eight every spring and has never been permitted to change it.

npcs.name: Faye Okonkwo

lines.text: I am told you keep the book.
I keep the book. Sit down, you are very tall and I am not standing up for anybody.
Nine thousand weddings and every one of them is a line in that book, and the book is the only thing in this town that has never once been wrong.

topics.label: Are there names in it that are not names?
replies: You are the second person to ask me that in sixty years and the first one was a policeman and he was not being kind.
Yes. Three of them, in one hand. Fifty-seven, eighty-four, twenty-eleven. Witness each time, never the couple.
It is not twenty-seven, it is eight and eight and eight and so on, and I did that arithmetic in nineteen ninety-two on the back of a gas bill and I have not been able to unknow it since.
It is not a signature, either. It is a mark. Two rings, one on top of the other, done without lifting the pen.

topics.label: Why does the book stay when nothing else does?
replies: Now that is the right question and nobody has ever asked it, so I have had to work out the answer on my own over about four decades.
Everything else in this town is an arrangement. The drinks, the money, the shows, the nights people cannot account for. None of it settles.
A signature is not an arrangement. It is somebody saying I was here, and putting their hand on it, and then somebody else saying yes, they were, and putting their hand on it too.
That holds. I do not know why it holds. It holds.

topics.label: Marla asked me to witness.
replies: Marla asks everyone. Marla asked a man with a parrot on Tuesday.
She is not wrong to. It costs you nothing and it is the only thing you will ever be able to do here that is still true in the morning.
Sign in the second column, and press. The pen is terrible and I will not be replacing it, it has outlasted three ministers.
And then it is in the book. And in eight years, or eighty, somebody will open it looking for something else and find you instead, and that is how it works and it is the whole of it.

topics.label: Four of them, tonight.
replies: She has the book open before you reach the desk.

Nine thousand and four. And four in a night has happened before — it happened in fifty-one and it happened the night of the fight — but four in a night out of people who walked in ALONE has not happened, and I have been sat at this desk for sixty years, so I would know.
Yes. That is what I do. Sit down.
Second column. Press hard, the pen is terrible and I will not be replacing it.
There. You are in it now, in your own hand, on a page with four couples who did not know each other at nine o’clock.
And in eight years, or eighty, somebody will open this book looking for something else and they will find you instead. That is how it works. That is the whole of how it works.

topics.label: Show me the page.
replies: Four lines, eight names and yours under all of them in the second column.
And do not go looking at the fifty-seven page tonight. One mystery an evening. I have waited thirty years, I can wait until you have had a coffee.

topics.label: I am here to sign.
replies: Sit down. Second column, and press — the pen is terrible and I will not be replacing it.
Names of the couple. Names of the witnesses. The date. That is the whole of it and it is the most binding thing in this town.
That is right.
...Fifty-seven. Eighty-four. Twenty-eleven. And tonight.
Nothing. Nothing at all. I have been at this desk sixty years and I am allowed to notice a thing without saying what I think of it.
Go on. It is done. And in eight years, or eighty, somebody will open this book looking for something else and find you instead, and that is how it works and it is the whole of it.

topics.label: The dates in the fifty-seven column.
replies: One hand. Three weddings, fifty-four years apart, witness each time and never the couple.
And now a fourth, in a different hand, by somebody who walked in here out of the weather and fixed a projector for a boy he had never met.
I am not saying anything. I am saying I have never lost a page and I am not starting tonight.

topics.label: Thank you, Faye.
replies: Do not thank me, sign the thing. — and come and see the fifty-seven page before you go. I have had it flat under glass for thirty years waiting for somebody to be able to read it.

npcs.bio: Sixty years behind the desk and keeper of the register. Has never lost a page and would like that written down somewhere.

npcs.name: Marisol Vance

lines.text: You run the light?
I keep it on. Different job. Nobody runs it, it has been on since before I was hired and the switch is welded.
You want to know the thing, do you. Everyone gets to the thing eventually. Mr Win took four years.

topics.label: Tell me the thing.
replies: It does not diffuse.
Every beam of light spreads. Always. It is not a rule somebody made up, it is what light is — go far enough and any beam is a smudge.
I have measured this one at ground level, at three thousand feet off the back of Roxy Calderon's aircraft, and once at eleven miles with a borrowed telescope and a very understanding friend.
Same width. All three. To the limit of what I can measure.
That is not a light, whatever else it is. Light does not do that. Something that has both its ends fixed does that.

topics.label: What is the separate supply for?
replies: Nathan tells the tourists it is redundancy. It is not redundancy, it is isolation, which is the opposite thing.

The plant down there is not sized to run a lamp. It is sized to refuse to give power to anything else. There are eight breakers in that room whose job is to make sure this building cannot be drained by the county.
I counted them the first week. I have never told anybody I counted them.

topics.label: What happens during the blackout?
replies: I have worked two. Whole valley goes and this stays, and it is the loneliest eight seconds you will ever spend.
And the beam does something. Not brighter. Not dimmer. It ticks — eight of them, about a second apart, like something very large tapping on a window.
You feel it in the handrail. I have stopped putting my hand on the handrail.

topics.label: Long night, Marisol.
replies: They are all long. — if you are going up onto the footing, go now while the tour is out. And put your hand flat on it, not your fingertips. Fingertips will not do it.

npcs.bio: Night engineer on the beam. Has measured it more carefully than anyone has ever asked her to.

npcs.name: Hollis Deane

lines.text: Quiet out here.
It is not quiet, it is empty. Different thing. Quiet stops.
You will want the wall. Everybody wants the wall. It is behind the register and I do not charge for it.

topics.label: Tonya Soprani.
replies: He puts the cloth down. He does not put it down quickly.
"Eight hundred dollars."

"I have been saying eight hundred dollars in my head every morning since March, in the shower, while I am doing the forecourt, and I have never once said it out loud until now, and it is smaller out loud."
"I know what she sends. I have filled their tank."

topics.label: Show me the wall.
replies: Forty-one of them. Instant film, because instant film cannot be argued with — no negative to lose, no lab to blame.
Lights over the flats, mostly. Two of a truck that was not there in the morning. One of a man standing at pump three at four a.m. who did not put any fuel in and did not drive away.
He is in the photograph. That is what happened to him. He is still in the photograph and he has not been anywhere else since nineteen ninety-nine.

topics.label: What goes up that road?
replies: Fuel. Regular as a heartbeat, and I am the only pump for seventy miles so I see all of it.
Diesel by the tanker. And it goes IN and nothing comes back out burnt, if you follow me — there is no plant up there, no stack, no heat. It is going down a hole.
Twenty-two years. That is a lot of diesel going down a hole.

topics.label: Have you been up to the fence?
replies: Once. Nineteen ninety-four, with a dog, because I had a dog then.
Dog would not go past the cattle grid. Not frightened — would not. Sat down in the road and looked at me like I had asked her to do arithmetic.
I have thought about that dog more than I have thought about most people.

topics.label: Fill her up.
replies: Nothing to fill, by the look of you. — if you are going up there, go along the south wire. It is newer than the posts, and newer wire means somebody put a hole in the old one.

npcs.bio: Runs the pumps on the highway. Has a wall of photographs and no particular theory about any of them.

npcs.name: Bobbie Lomax

lines.text: Is this thing still running?
Every night since fifty-nine. Three laps, four cars, and I write down who won.
You want the car in bay one, you take it off me three times. Not once. Three.

topics.label: Why three?
replies: Because anybody can have a night. My grandmother set it at three and my grandmother was not a sentimental woman.
Then it is yours and I sign it over, and the next fool who comes out here races for a different car.

topics.label: You said you write it down.
replies: Every result since fifty-nine, in the same book, in the same hand until my mother’s wrist went.
I read it. That is the whole of the audience and it is enough.
...You want to know something odd about this town? Almost nothing in it keeps. Ask anyone what they did on Tuesday.

Two places keep. That chapel on the Strip keeps its register, and I keep this. Whatever you do out on my track is still true in the morning, and I could not tell you why that is worth saying out loud, only that it is.

topics.label: Who am I racing?
replies: Dolly Vance, who is quick and knows it. Cutter Ames, who has never lifted for anybody in his life. And Mo Delgado, who will finish third and be perfectly happy about it.
They will lean on you at the top of the banking. Lean back. It is a stock car, it is supposed to have marks on it.

topics.label: What is all that stuff on the track?
replies: The arrows are mine. Compressor and a ramp, and if you put a wheel on one it will pick you up and put you down further along than you were expecting.

The oil is not mine, it is Cutter’s, and he has been told. You will keep every mile an hour you had and you will not be able to point the car anywhere for a second and a half. Do not fight it, just wait.
The drums are mine again. They mark where I do not want you and they are full of sand. Hit one at speed and you will be looking back down the straight you came up.
...Everything worth having out there is off the quick line. That is not an accident, that is the whole of the game.

topics.label: Later.
replies: Flag is here when you are. It is always here.

npcs.bio: Clerk of the course at the Eight Mile. Holds the flag, holds the book, and has never once been persuaded to lose either.

npcs.name: Roy Ellinger

lines.text: You are still running it.
Six nights. Same programme since the Tuesday I started, and I have stopped saying that out loud because of how people look at me.
You are the first thing through that door in a long while that I have wanted to show something to.

topics.label: Show me what, exactly?
replies: There is a frame in the print that is not in the print.
Then she is not mad and neither am I, and that is the best news I have had since nineteen ninety-one.
Reel three. Two thirds of the way in, between a man closing a door and the same man on the other side of it. One frame that belongs to neither.

topics.label: Cut it out, then.
replies: I have. Four times, four different prints, and I am good at it — you would not find my splices with a loupe.
It comes back. Not in the same place in the reel. In the same place in the NIGHT. About eleven minutes past ten, whatever I am running.
...Which tells you it was never on the film. Something is putting it on the light on the way across that lot, and the emulsion is only what writes it down.

topics.label: What is on the frame?
replies: That is the thing. I have had it under the loupe two hundred times and I could not draw it for you now.
Rings. Two of them, one sitting over the other, and the top one smaller. Not one straight line in the whole of it.
Then he has got further than me, because I can hold it for about a second and a half and then it is gone, like a name.
On a loupe it is four millimetres across. That is the problem. You want it sixty feet across, and I happen to own the only wall in the state that will take it.

topics.label: Why has nobody else seen it?
replies: Because it is one frame in twenty-four and because this is a town where nobody finishes a sentence about anything.
And because the two men who did see it stopped coming. Not moved away. Stopped coming — one of them worked in the snack bar and I never saw him walk out of it.
I have thought about that for a long time and I have kept running the picture, because the alternative was to sit up here and not.

topics.label: There is a couple on the Strip waiting on the second feature.
replies: The second feature.
I know what the second feature is. It is four feet from your elbow and it has been four feet from my elbow for forty-one years.
Because the first one does not finish. You cannot put the second feature up in the middle of the first, and the first one has not got to the end of itself since the Tuesday I started.
A young man has been out here asking. Four times. I have given him the tide speech four times and I have not once believed it.
So. You take it down and you go and stand on the lot, and we will find out together whether this town lets a thing finish.

topics.label: Later, Roy.
replies: The lamp is warm. It is always warm.

npcs.bio: Forty-one years in this booth. Has spliced the same frame out of four different prints and watched it come back in all four.

npcs.name: Del Marchetti

lines.text: Busy night.
It is the same night. I have got forty orders out there and I have never once collected a tray.
Do not park in row nine. Everybody says that and nobody says why.

topics.label: Why not row nine?
replies: Because the cars in it are cold and the cars either side of it are warm. Bonnets. You can feel it going down the row.
Then she is sitting on the same line I am skating across, and I would like to buy her a drink and talk about something else.
Nine is straight out from the port. Roy could tell you that to the inch. I only know it because my skates pull.

topics.label: Forty orders?
replies: Onion rings mostly. I take them out, I put them on the window, and the next time I look the tray is on the post and the rings are gone and the window is up.
Somebody is TAKING them. There is a difference and I have had a lot of time to think about it.

topics.label: Who is in the Buick in row four?
replies: Wendell and Arletta. They are lovely and I would not go over there if I were you.
Because they will ask you what time the second picture starts and you will not have an answer, and then you will be standing there.

topics.label: Nothing, thanks.
replies: Then you are the only one out here who wants nothing.

npcs.bio: Carhop on skates. Knows every car on this lot by its order and not one of them by its driver.

npcs.name: Wendell Pike

lines.text: Good picture?
The first one was. We are waiting on the second. They put the lights up in between, you know.
Arletta says I am not to ask anybody the time. So I will not ask you the time.

topics.label: How long have you been waiting?
replies: Since the interval. They ran the trailers, they ran the thing about the snack bar with the dancing hot dog, and then it went to black.
It is. And I have been sitting in it enjoying myself, and the only thing that bothers me is that I have not once needed to shift in this seat.

topics.label: What was the first picture?
replies: It was — hm.
It was very good. I remember laughing at the front of it and I remember Arletta putting her hand on my arm at the end.
Not the picture. And I am going to sit here until they run the second one, because if I go home now I will have driven out for nothing.

topics.label: You should go home, Wendell.
replies: That is what the girl on the skates says.
...You want to know the thing I do not say to Arletta? The road back into town has a bend in it and I cannot picture the bend.
I can picture this lot. I can picture that screen. Everything the other way is a sort of — going.
So we shall wait for the second picture. It is a nice night and it has always been a nice night.

topics.label: That was the second one, Wendell.
replies: It was. It was, was it not.
They put the lights up in between. I told you they put the lights up in between and nobody believed me.
No. No, and I find I do not mind at all, which Arletta says is the most me thing I have ever said.
She has gone very quiet. She has hold of my arm. I think she liked it.

topics.label: Enjoy the film.
replies: We shall. Any minute now.

npcs.bio: Came out for the double feature. The first picture finished a long time ago and he is not going anywhere until the second one starts.

npcs.name: Arletta Pike

lines.text: Evening.
Evening. Do not tell him what time it is. He will only start counting.

topics.label: You know, then.
replies: I know the moon has not moved.
I noticed it against the top corner of that screen the first night and I have checked it — I could not tell you how many times, and that is the other thing I know.
What would I be giving him? He is happy. He is holding my hand in a car at the pictures. I have had worse for ever.

topics.label: Do you want to leave?
replies: I have tried it. Twice.
You drive out to the road and the road is there and the bend is there and then you are turning in at the STARLITE sign and Wendell is saying we should get here early for the double.
The second time I watched the mirror the whole way round so I would see it happen. I did not see it happen.

topics.label: What would help?
replies: Somebody running the second picture.
That is all. Something has to FINISH here. Ask anyone on this lot what they are waiting for and you will get forty answers and they are all the same answer.
The man up in the booth has a reel he will not run. I have never asked him why and I think it is because I am frightened of what a sensible reason would mean.

topics.label: Something finished.
replies: Something finished.
I have been sitting in this car for — I am not going to say the number out loud, because he is right there and he counts.
And tonight a picture started and it ran and it stopped, and the lights came up, and that is the first edge I have found in this place since we turned in at the sign.
Yes. Not because it will help. Because I have been carrying it on my own and tonight there is something else in the evening besides me.
You did that. I asked you for one thing and you went and did it, and nobody has done a thing I asked for in a very long while.

topics.label: Goodnight.
replies: Goodnight. Mind the posts, they are lower than they look.

npcs.bio: Has worked out rather more than her husband has, and has decided that telling him would not improve either of their evenings.

npcs.name: Ruth Ambrose

lines.text: Are you open?
Always. That is not a slogan, it is a rota with one name on it.
Bring me anything. I will give you a fair price and a ticket, and the ticket is good for ninety days.
And if you are not here about a ticket, say so now, quietly, and look at me while you say it.

topics.label: Who are the two by the door?
replies: Security.
For a pawn shop.
I have four hundred tickets on that wall and not one of them has been collected in eleven years, love. What exactly do you think is being secured?

topics.label: I am here about Ryan.
replies: One hundred thousand dollars.

She is through the back. Do not tell her I said any of that. She knows I said it. Do not tell her anyway.

replies: Tickets. Every one is something somebody left with me meaning to come back inside ninety days.
None.
